Monte Carlo Sensitivity Analysis for Sequential AIPE Procedures

Source: R/sensitivity.R
seq_aipe_sensitivity.Rd

Each function runs a sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) procedure from its pilot sample to its stopping point G times, against a data generating mechanism whose true effect size is known, and summarizes the final sample size, the width of the final confidence interval, and how often that interval contains the true value. Use them before data collection to see what a planned study should expect: how large the sample is likely to become, how variable that is, and whether the confidence interval can be trusted at the planned width.

Usage

seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("gamma", "lognormal"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_sm_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_gini_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_aipe_c_sensitivity(
  true_means,
  contrast_weights,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  true_sds = 1,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

Arguments

true_value

The population value of the effect size under the data generating mechanism: the standardized mean difference (any finite number), the correlation (strictly between -1 and 1), the coefficient of variation (positive), the regression slope (any finite number), the standardized mean (any finite number), or the Gini index (strictly between 0 and 1). Within those ranges, a value at which the generated data would have too little variation to be used is an error. The check functions take a sample whose values agree to ten significant digits to have no variation, and the sensitivity functions keep the generated data a factor of 100 clear of that: the standardized mean difference and the standardized mean must be less than 1e8 in absolute value (the data have unit variance), the coefficient of variation must be greater than 1e-8, and the Gini index greater than about 5.6e-9. The regression slope must be less than 1 / .Machine$double.eps (about 4.5e15) in absolute value, beside which the unit variance of the errors cannot be represented. A coefficient of variation or Gini index so large that its generating parameter (see Details) is not a positive finite number is an error as well.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval (the quantity \(\omega\) of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay, 2018, 2019), in the units of the effect size. For the contrast these are the units of the response. For the correlation it must be less than 2, and for the Gini index less than 1, the lengths of their ranges.

conf_level

The confidence level, strictly between 0 and 1 (default 0.95).

distribution

The data generating mechanism (see Details). "normal" or "skewed" for the standardized mean difference, the correlation, the regression slope, the standardized mean, and the contrast; "gamma" or "lognormal" for the coefficient of variation. The Gini index function always generates lognormal data and has no such argument.

G

The number of Monte Carlo replications, a whole number of at least 1 (default 1000). See Details for the Monte Carlo error this implies.

seed

NULL (the default) or a single whole number. With a number the result is reproducible, and the caller's random number stream is left exactly as it was found. With NULL the draws come from the current stream.

m_0

The minimum pilot sample size, a whole number of at least 4 (default 4), passed to the matching seq_aipe_*_pilot() function. The pilot sample size is the larger of m_0 and \(\lceil 2 z/\omega \rceil\), where \(z\) is the standard normal quantile for conf_level (1.96 at 0.95). Like every sample size here (max_n, batch, and the rows mean_n, median_n, and sd_n), it counts observations per group for the standardized mean difference and the contrast, pairs for the correlation and the regression slope, and observations otherwise.

max_n

The largest sample size a replication may reach, in the unit described under m_0 (per group, for example, for the standardized mean difference and the contrast, not in total): a whole number no smaller than the pilot sample size (default 100,000). A replication that has not met the stopping rule at max_n is stopped there, exactly, whatever the batch size (the last batch is shortened). It is an error for max_n to be below the pilot sample size. The row pct_hit_max_n reports how often the cap, not the rule, ended a replication; when it is above zero the other rows describe a truncated procedure and should be read with care.

batch

The number of observations added between checks of the stopping rule after the pilot sample, a whole number of at least 1 (default 1; see Details), in the unit described under m_0: for the standardized mean difference and the contrast it is the number added to every group; for the correlation and the regression slope it is the number of pairs.

true_means

For the contrast: the population means, one per group (at least two groups), each less than 1e8 times its group's standard deviation in absolute value (for the reason given under true_value).

contrast_weights

For the contrast: the contrast coefficients \(c_k\), one per group and not all zero, as in seq_aipe_c. true_means, contrast_weights, and true_sds (when it has one entry per group) are matched to the groups by position; if more than one of them is named, the names must be the same and in the same order, or the function stops.

true_sds

For the contrast: the population standard deviations, either one positive number shared by every group (default 1) or one per group. Their squares must be positive finite numbers.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_sensitivity", "data.frame"): a data frame with columns term (character) and value (numeric) that can be used as any data frame, with a print() method that shows every value in fixed notation (see smsd_sensitivity_methods). It has these 13 rows, in this order:

true_value

The population value of the effect size. For the contrast, the contrast of true_means.

target_width

The requested full width, width.

conf_level

The confidence level, a proportion.

replications

The number of replications run, G.

mean_n, median_n, sd_n

The mean, median, and standard deviation of the final sample size across replications: observations for the coefficient of variation, the standardized mean, and the Gini index; pairs for the correlation and the regression slope; observations per group for the standardized mean difference and the contrast. sd_n is NA when G is 1.

mean_width, median_width

The mean and median full width of the final confidence interval, in the units of the effect size, over the replications that ended with an interval (see below); NA when none did.

pct_width_within

The percentage (0 to 100) of replications whose final interval is no wider than width.

coverage

The proportion (0 to 1) of replications whose final interval contains the true value.

pct_hit_max_n

The percentage (0 to 100) of replications stopped by max_n before the stopping rule was met.

pct_variance_unusable

The percentage (0 to 100) of replications in which, at one or more checks, the check function reported its variance estimate as unusable: the raw estimate was zero, negative, or not finite, so that no variance had been estimated and the stopping rule was reported as not met at that check. A replication is counted once however many of its checks were of this kind, and the check at which max_n ended it counts as well. A positive estimate, however small, is usable and is not counted.

A replication that the stopping rule ends always has an interval. A replication that max_n ends can finish on a check that gives no interval, because the estimate is not finite or the variance estimate is unusable (the check function then reports its limits as NA). Such a replication counts as not covering and as not within the target width, so that coverage and pct_width_within remain proportions of all G replications; it is left out of mean_width and median_width; and it is counted like any other in the remaining rows, pct_hit_max_n among them. No row becomes NA on this account, except the two width rows when not one replication ended with an interval.

Details

One call does what the pilot, collect, and check loop does by hand: it draws the pilot sample that the matching pilot function gives, evaluates the stopping rule with the matching check function, adds batch observations, and repeats until the rule is met or the sample reaches max_n.

Data generating mechanisms. The true value is exact for each mechanism.

  • seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(): two independent groups with unit variance, the first with mean true_value and the second with mean 0.

  • seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(): pairs \((x, y)\) with \(y = \rho x + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, e\), where \(x\) and \(e\) are independent with unit variance and \(\rho\) is true_value. The procedure studied is the Pearson correlation.

  • seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(): \(y = \beta x + e\), where \(x\) and \(e\) are independent with unit variance and \(\beta\) is true_value.

  • seq_aipe_sm_sensitivity(): one sample with mean true_value and unit variance.

  • seq_aipe_c_sensitivity(): independent groups with means true_means and standard deviations true_sds. The true value is the contrast \(\sum_k c_k \mu_k\). The groups are balanced, as seq_aipe_c requires: each addition is batch observations from every group.

  • seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity(): gamma data with shape \(1/\kappa^2\), or lognormal data with log standard deviation \(\sqrt{\log(1 + \kappa^2)}\), where \(\kappa\) is true_value.

  • seq_aipe_gini_sensitivity(): lognormal data with log standard deviation \(\sqrt{2}\,\Phi^{-1}((g + 1)/2)\), where \(g\) is true_value and \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the standard normal quantile function.

For the first five, distribution = "normal" draws the unit variance variables from the standard normal distribution and distribution = "skewed" draws them from a chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, standardized to mean 0 and variance 1 (skewness about 1.63).

Batch size. With batch = 1, the default, the stopping rule is checked after every observation. That is the purely sequential procedure, and it is what the simulations of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, 2019) use; batch is the quantity they call \(m'\) (2018, Figure 1). A study that can check only after every 5, 10, or 20 observations stops later than the first sample size at which the rule would have been met; set batch to that number to see the overshoot to expect. For a standardized mean difference of 0.5 at width = 0.4, for example, the mean final sample size per group was 199.1 with batch = 1, 201.2 with 5, 203.6 with 10, and 209.5 with 20 (4,700 to 6,000 replications each, standard errors about 0.1), and coverage stayed between 0.949 and 0.952: checking less often cost about half a batch per group.

Coverage is an asymptotic property. The procedures deliver the requested width by construction: the final interval is never wider than width unless max_n ends the replication first. Coverage is a different matter. The articles prove that it approaches conf_level as width shrinks (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, p. 232; 2019, p. 495), that is, as the sample that the stopping rule asks for grows. When that sample is small, coverage can fall well short of conf_level. How small it is depends on the true value as well as on width: a strong correlation is estimated with so little sampling error that the rule is met in a small sample even at a width that would be narrow for a moderate correlation.

The table gives what these functions measured at conf_level = 0.95, with the defaults and normal data unless a distribution is named: the mean final sample size (the row mean_n), the coverage, and the percentage of replications in which the variance estimate was unusable at one or more checks (the row pct_variance_unusable, explained below). Each row rests on 800 to 34,000 replications; the Monte Carlo standard error of the coverage is below 0.008 in every row but three with a mean n above 800 (the correlation of 0.9 at 0.025, the slope of 2 at 0.1, and the lognormal coefficient of variation at 0.05), where it is 0.009 to 0.012.

(The contrast has weights 1, -0.5, and -0.5, means 0.5, 0, and 0, and unit standard deviations. The coverage for the Gini index is that of the interval seq_aipe_gini reports. The fixed width interval of Chattopadhyay and De, 2016, the estimate plus and minus half the width, contained the index in 0.986 and 0.960 of the same studies; see seq_aipe_gini.) These values hold for the true values shown, not for an effect size in general: the rows for a correlation of 0.9 and for a slope of 2 are far from those for a correlation of 0.4 and a slope of 0.5, at widths that are no wider. Skewed data can lower coverage further: for a slope of 0.5 at width = 0.4 it was 0.71 with the skewed data.

Read the coverage row before relying on an interval at a planned width, and run the function at each true value that is plausible for the study, the strongest included. When coverage is low, plan a narrower width (a larger study), raise the minimum pilot size m_0, or both. With m_0 = 40 at width = 0.4, coverage rose from 0.78 to 0.90 for a correlation of 0.4 and from 0.83 to 0.92 for a slope of 0.5, while the mean final sample size rose from 55 to 64 and from 80 to 90. A larger pilot sample is a weaker remedy when the true value is strong: for a correlation of 0.9 at width = 0.1, m_0 = 100 raised coverage only from 0.45 to 0.69.

When the variance estimate is unusable. In a small sample the raw estimate of the asymptotic variance can be zero, negative, or not finite: no variance has been estimated. The check functions report such a check as not met and set the attribute variance_unusable to TRUE, so sampling continues (see smsd_check_methods; this is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the articles, under which the procedure would stop at once with an interval far narrower than the data support). A positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe and is not counted here.

The row pct_variance_unusable is the percentage of replications in which this happened at one or more checks; it is the last column of the table. Like coverage, it depends on the true value as well as on the width, and it is not confined to wide targets or to one effect size. It was 16 percent for a correlation of 0.4 at width = 0.4 but 79 percent for a correlation of 0.9 at width = 0.1; 20 percent for a slope of 0.5 at width = 0.4 but 65 percent for a slope of 2 at width = 0.2; and 15 percent for a standardized mean of 1 at width = 1, where coverage was 0.86. With the skewed data it was 37 percent for the slope of 0.5 at width = 0.4.

Continuing past such a check does not by itself make the final interval trustworthy. The estimate on which a replication finally stops can still be far too small, which makes the final interval too narrow: for the correlation of 0.9 at width = 0.1, the final intervals had a mean width of 0.028, about a third of the 0.086 that the true variance gives at the mean final sample size, and their coverage was 0.45. With a very strong relationship the estimate can also stay unusable for a long time. For a correlation of 0.99 at width = 0.1 (a pilot sample of 40), 20 replications ended at a mean of 7,500 pairs, each taking about 6.5 seconds on the computer used for these runs, and 1 of their 20 final intervals contained the true value. Set max_n when exploring such conditions, and read pct_hit_max_n.

Monte Carlo error. Every summary is an estimate from G replications. The standard error of coverage is about \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/G}\) for a coverage of \(p\): 0.007 at the default G = 1000 and 0.002 at G = 10000 when \(p\) is near 0.95. The standard error of mean_n is sd_n divided by \(\sqrt{G}\).

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203

Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within pre-specified error bound. Econometrics, 4(3), 30. doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

Examples

# G is kept very small in these examples so that they run in a fraction
# of a second, and the targets are wide for the same reason. A planning
# result that will be reported deserves G = 10000, at the width the
# study will use.

# A training program compared with a control group; the true
# standardized mean difference in engagement is 0.5.
seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 1.2, G = 10, seed = 113)
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.5
#> target_width           1.2
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           10
#> mean_n                 23.8
#> median_n               23
#> sd_n                   1.932184
#> mean_width             1.170544
#> median_width           1.171495
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               1
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  0

# Job satisfaction and performance ratings with a true correlation of
# 0.4. Ten replications say little about coverage (its standard error
# here is about 0.15); in 10,000 replications at this very wide target
# it was 0.65, far below 0.95.
